description_ru: Ироничное эссе о том, почему скука, которую мы так старательно изгоняем смартфонами, оказывается плодородной почвой для воображения.
text:
There was a time, not so very long ago, when a person waiting for a train had nothing to do but wait. He would stand upon the platform, shifting his weight from one foot to the other, studying the advertisements, the pigeons and the faces of strangers, and sooner or later his mind, deprived of occupation, would begin to wander off on errands of its own. We call this state boredom, and we have recently decided that it is a kind of illness, a malfunction to be corrected with all available technology. I should like, in the spirit of contrarianism, to propose that it is nothing of the sort.

Consider the modern predicament. In the history of our species there has never been a generation so thoroughly armed against tedium. We carry in our pockets an infinite library, a cinema, a gossip column, a casino and a bazaar, and we consult them every few minutes with the anxious devotion of a patient taking his pulse. A gap of ten seconds at a pedestrian crossing, a lull in conversation, the brief interval between the kettle being switched on and the water boiling: each is promptly stuffed with a flicker of electronic distraction, as though silence were a hole in the road into which one might fall.

The curious result is that we are, by every account, more bored than ever. Boredom has not been defeated; it has merely been driven underground, where it festers as a vague and persistent restlessness. This should not surprise us. A person who never allows himself to be hungry will never taste his dinner, and a person who never permits himself to be bored will never discover what it is that he actually wants. Boredom is the hunger of the mind, and like hunger it has a function: it tells us that the current menu is unsatisfactory and that something better had better be found.

The great creative figures of history, whatever else they disagreed upon, seem to have been united in their devotion to idleness. Darwin took a walk along his sandwalk, a gravel path at the bottom of his garden, every afternoon, circling it in a trance of apparently aimless thought. Newton, so the story goes, was sitting idly in an orchard when an apple fell. Archimedes had his epiphany in the bath, which is the natural habitat of the idle, and the poet Coleridge, who was interrupted at the crucial moment by a visitor from Porlock, never finished the dream that became Kubla Khan. None of these gentlemen was monitoring his notifications.

Psychologists, who have an unfortunate habit of confirming what grandmothers have always known, now supply the data. Experiments have shown that people who are made to perform a tedious task, such as copying numbers from a telephone directory, subsequently produce more original ideas than those who were allowed to remain stimulated. The explanation appears to be that when the mind is not preoccupied, it slips into a mode of free association, a sort of internal daydream, in which remote memories and unconnected facts collide and occasionally marry. Novelty, it turns out, is born in the vacant lot rather than the factory floor.

There is also a moral argument, which I offer with some trepidation, since moral arguments are rarely welcomed at breakfast. A person who cannot tolerate being bored cannot tolerate himself. He needs a companion, a screen, a murmuring radio or a stream of other people's opinions, because the alternative is an unscheduled encounter with his own thoughts, and these may be less flattering than he would like. Pascal observed three centuries ago that all of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone. He had not even met the smartphone.

Nor is the problem confined to adults. I have watched a restaurant in which four children, aged perhaps between five and ten, sat in a row at a table, each hypnotised by a glowing rectangle, while their parents, with the expression of well-meaning hostages, ate their soup in silence. The parents, I suspect, were doing their best. A bored child is an irritating child, and a tablet is an efficient anaesthetic. But I fear we are depriving the young of a crucial apprenticeship. It is during long, tedious afternoons, with nothing to play with, that children invent a game involving a sofa cushion, a wooden spoon and a fictional tribe of warriors.

Let me not be misunderstood. I am no Luddite, and I would not abolish the internet any more than I would abolish the post. Some boredom is merely grim: the dreary hours of a hospital waiting room, or of an unrewarding job, are not likely to be mistaken for creative incubation. The point is not that tedium is always delightful but that it is sometimes productive, and that we have developed a reflex for extinguishing it before it has had a chance to bear fruit. We behave like a gardener who digs up every seed to check that it is growing.

What, then, is to be done? I propose a modest, almost embarrassingly low-tech remedy. Once a day, for a quarter of an hour, one should sit somewhere with nothing in one's hands: no book, no phone, no podcast, not even a cup of coffee to give the fingers something to do. One should look out of the window. For the first five minutes the experience will be unpleasant, rather like a long-delayed conversation with an estranged relative. The mind will fidget, grumble, compile shopping lists and demand its phone back. One should resist.

Then, somewhere around the tenth minute, something happens. The restlessness subsides, the fidgeting ceases, and a certain spaciousness opens up, in which odd and delightful thoughts begin to arrive unbidden: a half-forgotten melody, a solution to a problem that has been vexing one for a week, the sudden memory of a seaside holiday, a plan. It is difficult to describe, and I would hesitate to call it a revelation. It is more like the sensation of a house in which someone has finally opened the windows.

The enemies of boredom are legion and well funded, and they have no interest in your reflection, since a reflective person is a poor consumer. I urge you, therefore, to be a little more subversive. Stand on the platform. Study the pigeons. Let the train be late. The most interesting thing in the vicinity, I promise you, is the mind that you have been so assiduously avoiding.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Кончик языка между зубами, голос включён; артикль the почти всегда звучит с этим звуком.
Язык между зубами, голоса нет; не заменяйте на «с», «ф» или «т».
Язык поднят к мягкому нёбу, воздух идёт через нос; не произносите отдельное «г» в конце.
Подчёркивайте ударный слог и сокращайте остальные до ə; в слове companion ударение падает на второй слог.

questions.question: What does the author say boredom really is?
questions.answer: The hunger of the mind, a useful signal.

questions.question: Which famous thinkers does the author mention as idle?
What remedy does the author propose?
questions.answer: Sitting for a quarter of an hour with nothing in your hands.

questions.question: What did Pascal observe?
questions.answer: That man's problems come from being unable to sit quietly in a room alone.
